newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: European car makers face profit squeeze.
newsitem.headline: European car makers face profit squeeze.

text.p: European car manufacturers' profit margins will come under yet more pressure this year and the companies can only blame themselves, industry analysts say.
As the industry gathers here for the annual car show, current conditions suggest that the companies should almost have a license to print money, as car sales creep back towards record highs.

But, the industry's failure to bite the bullet of overcapacity has condemned it to an endless spiral of beggar-thy-neighbour cost cutting. To keep plants running at close to capacity, car companies have engaged in a ruinous slashing of prices and expensive incentives that are almost the equivalent of buying sales.

"Excess capacity of between two and four million cars has led to intensified competition, with government incentives often being matched by adding free or discounted options," Gregory Melich, automotive analyst with Morgan Stanley said in a recent report.
For a year ended last September, the French government offered rebates to buyers who traded in old clunkers for new, cleaner cars. Italy announced a similar scheme starting in January.
Analysts say these schemes have no long term impact on sales, but merely steal sales from a later period, and concentrate purchasing on smaller, cheaper and less profitable models.
Recent news suggests that the car makers are gritting their teeth and starting to take tough decisions on production.

On Thursday last week, France's Renault SA announced it would close a factory at Vilvoorde, near Brussels, with the loss of 3,100 jobs. In January, Ford Motor Co said it would slash 980 jobs at its Halewood, England plant. The political storm following both these actions underlines why car companies are reluctant to take these tough decisions.
But lots more needs to be done.
"Although sales were almost back to peak levels in 1996, profit margins are still a long way from historic peaks," said Sabinel Blumel, senior analyst at stockbrokers IMI Sigeco.
Car sales in western Europe peaked at 13.5 million in 1992, but plummeted almost two million or 15 percent the following year, the biggest drop in sales for 50 years.
Since then sales have struggled to regain the record pace, and in 1996 had crept back up to around 12.8 million. Most experts expect sales to just top 13 million in 1997.
"In a cyclical industry like car assembly, profit margins are a function of sales volumes and are directly correlated to the utilisation level of production........ overcapacity, both
in Europe and worldwide is a cause of low profitability for the industry," Blumel said.

"The margin squeeze is structural and the profit margins of the west European volume car manufacturers are unlikely to recover in future cycles. It is a dynamic process which is likely to last well into the next decade," Blumel said.
Some companies are doing better than others though.

In a report, the Economist Intelligence Unit of London said General Motors Corp, with its Opel and Vauxhall brands, was the most profitable car company of Europe's big six car mass manufacturers. GM Europe was expected to raise net profit in 1997 to 968 million ECU ($1.1 billion) from 1996's 545 million.

European market leader Volkswagen AG of Germany was said to be making progress. Like other analysts, the E.I.U. was scrambling to downgrade expectations at France's Renault, after the company issued a profit warning last month.
Analysts worry that Renault's losses may reach four billion francs ($699.5 million) in 1996.

According to the E.I.U., profits will be thin at Peugeot, the second French mass maker. Italy's Fiat SpA will do a litttle better. Ford Europe lost around $300 million in 1996, but should earn around $400 million in 1997.
The E.I.U. said Ford's U.S. parent was losing patience.
"Ford of Europe's losses are increasingly contrasting unfavourably with profits made by Ford in the USA, and it is clear that impatience with the European performance is growing," the E.I.U. said.
Ford has also been at the forefront of the discount wars.

"Marketing costs as a percentage of revenue (at Ford Europe) are almost 2-1/2 times those in the USA and it is clear that the company's cost position is unable to support this without heavy losses," the report said.
E.I.U. consultant Colin Whitbread said long-term profitability could only be restored by shutting down factories.

"The solution is that capacity has to be taken out, every company wants to do that, but if you take it out, it not only helps me, it helps my competition too. Nobody wants to be the first one to jump," Whitbread said.
